title: Sending Secrets Without Sharing a Secret First

sources.title: RFC 9180 — Hybrid Public Key Encryption
sources.notes: Introduces hybrid asymmetric/symmetric designs and KEM/KDF/AEAD composition. Episode distinguishes its conceptual wrapped-key teaching model from exact HPKE.

sources.title: RFC 5116 — An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption
sources.notes: AEAD confidentiality/integrity interface, authentication failure, and scheme-specific nonce requirements.

sources.title: RFC 8446 — TLS 1.3
sources.notes: TLS1.3 uses authenticated key establishment and AEAD; static RSA key transport removed. Used to distinguish the simplified diagram from modern TLS.

sections.title: A secret on a public network
sections.narration: Alice wants to send Bob a private message. Eve is the nosy person watching the network. If Alice sends the secret key openly too, Eve gets the answer sheet. Let's see how we can do better.
sections.takeaway: A public network needs more than a promise that nobody is listening.

sections.title: Plaintext becomes ciphertext
sections.narration: Encryption uses a key to turn a readable message, called plaintext, into ciphertext. The right key helps recover it. These moving letter blocks show the idea. They're an illustration, not a secret encryption method invented for this video.
bullets: Illustrated symbols are not real crypto
sections.takeaway: Encryption conceals content through a keyed transformation.

sections.title: The algorithm can be public
sections.narration: Here's a surprise: the algorithm doesn't need to be secret. A good design can let people study how it works while keeping the key secret. Hiding the instructions isn't the same as having a strong lock.
bullets: Secrecy of design is not a foundation
sections.takeaway: Protect the key rather than relying on an unknown algorithm.

sections.title: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret
sections.narration: With symmetric encryption, Alice and Bob share secret key material. They both need the correct key. Eve can know the method and see the ciphertext without knowing that secret. The key is doing an important job here.
sections.takeaway: A symmetric key must remain secret from unauthorized parties.

sections.title: A key is not simply a memorable password
sections.narration: A key like 'password123' wouldn't make us feel relaxed. Proper cryptographic keys need suitable length and unpredictability. Passwords need special processing too. Our little key drawings stand for properly generated keys, not short words we guessed over lunch.
sections.takeaway: Use appropriate key generation rather than a memorable homemade key.

sections.title: The key-distribution problem
sections.narration: Watch what happens when the shared key leaks. Eve can copy it and recover the message. The encryption hasn't suddenly forgotten its job. We've given away the secret it depended on, like leaving the key beside the lock.
bullets: Sending K openly reveals the secret
sections.takeaway: Secure encryption still needs a sound way to establish or distribute keys.

sections.title: Give Bob a pair of keys
sections.narration: Public-key encryption gives Bob two related keys. The public one can be shared; the private one stays with Bob. In a suitable scheme, data protected using his public key can be recovered with his private key.
sections.takeaway: A public/private key pair assigns different capabilities to each key.

sections.title: Publish the encryption key
sections.narration: Eve can get Bob's public key too. That alone doesn't give her his private key. But Alice must check whose public key she's using. A key saying 'Bob' on it isn't automatically proof that it belongs to him.
bullets: Public also does not mean trusted
sections.takeaway: Public-key distribution and public-key authentication are different problems.

sections.title: Encrypt to Bob’s public key
sections.narration: Alice uses Bob's authenticated public key to protect the message. Eve may see that key and the ciphertext, but lacks Bob's private decryption ability, assuming the scheme is sound. Seeing the package isn't the same as opening it.
bullets: Observing PK_B does not reveal SK_B
sections.takeaway: Use a suitable scheme and the intended recipient’s authenticated public key.

sections.title: Decrypt with the private key
sections.narration: Bob uses his private key to recover the protected information. That private key stays private; it doesn't travel inside the message. If it gets stolen, the damage depends on how the protocol uses its keys.
bullets: The private key is not transmitted
sections.takeaway: Protecting private keys is part of protecting the communication.

sections.title: Why not encrypt every file this way?
sections.narration: Why not use public-key operations for every bit of a huge file? They have practical costs and limits. Hybrid designs combine the strengths: public-key tools help with keys, while symmetric encryption handles the bulk of the data efficiently.
sections.takeaway: Hybrid designs combine complementary capabilities.

sections.title: Generate a fresh session key
sections.narration: Alice generates a fresh random session key, K. It's a key for this exchange, rather than one we casually reuse everywhere. Fresh keys help, but we still need the right checks and careful handling around them.
bullets: Generate fresh random session key K
sections.takeaway: A hybrid example begins with appropriate session key material.

sections.title: Protect the data with the session key
sections.narration: Now K helps protect the message and create an authentication tag. Think of the tag as a check tied to the secret key, not a decoration. The scheme also specifies any nonce and other information the receiver needs.
sections.takeaway: Authenticated symmetric encryption protects the bulk message.

sections.title: Protect the session key for Bob
sections.narration: In our simplified model, Alice protects K using Bob's authenticated public key. This is a way to explain protected key transport. Modern systems may establish keys differently, so don't treat our wrapped-key picture as an exact TLS handshake.
bullets: PK_B protects the small session key
This is a simplified key-transport model
sections.takeaway: Protect the session key separately from the bulk ciphertext.

sections.title: Send the two protected pieces
sections.narration: Two protected pieces travel: the key material and the authenticated ciphertext. Eve can see the packages without learning the message under the scheme's assumptions. But things like message size, timing, and the endpoints may still be visible.
bullets: Send protected key material and data
sections.takeaway: Ciphertext can conceal content while revealing other communication patterns.

sections.title: Bob recovers the key, then the message
sections.narration: Bob recovers K, then verifies and decrypts the protected data. If verification fails, reject it. A message that looks readable isn't enough reason to trust it. Checking the protection is part of the process, not an optional extra.
bullets: K authenticates and decrypts the data
sections.takeaway: A hybrid receiver verifies the protected data before accepting its contents.

sections.title: Secrecy alone does not detect tampering
sections.narration: Keeping a message secret and spotting changes are different jobs. Encryption alone doesn't automatically make tampering detectable. A suitable authenticated scheme supplies both confidentiality and integrity: hide the content, and detect unauthorized changes to the protected data.
sections.takeaway: Encryption and integrity are related but distinct security goals.

sections.title: An authentication tag checks the package
sections.narration: Let's change part of the protected message. The receiver's tag check should fail. This isn't an ordinary checksum that Eve can simply recalculate after editing the data. The authentication check depends on the key and the protected inputs.
bullets: A checksum is not a keyed authenticator
sections.takeaway: Authenticated encryption detects invalid protected packages.

sections.title: Do not reuse nonces carelessly
sections.narration: A nonce is another important input, but it isn't another secret key. Many schemes need a unique nonce each time a key is used. Repeating the wrong key-and-nonce pair can break protection, so follow that scheme's rules carefully.
bullets: A nonce is separate from the key
sections.takeaway: Correct nonce handling is essential to secure authenticated encryption.

sections.title: A substituted public key changes everything
sections.narration: Here's an attack: Eve replaces Bob's public key with her own. Alice's encryption may work perfectly, but now it's protecting the message for Eve. That's why checking who owns a public key matters as much as using it.
sections.takeaway: A public key is useful only with an appropriate trust decision.

sections.title: Confidentiality is not a sender’s signature
sections.narration: If anyone gets Bob's public encryption key, anyone can encrypt something for him. Bob successfully decrypting it doesn't prove Alice sent it. Digital signatures provide a separate way to check a claimed sender using signing and verification schemes.
bullets: Encrypting for Bob does not identify Alice
sections.takeaway: Recipient confidentiality does not automatically authenticate the sender.

sections.title: How this differs from modern TLS
sections.narration: Modern TLS one point three commonly uses authenticated temporary key exchange to derive traffic keys, then authenticated encryption. It removed static RSA key transport. Our wrapped-key drawing is a teaching model, not an exact TLS walkthrough.
sections.takeaway: Use the hybrid idea to understand protocols without confusing their mechanisms.

sections.title: Use established cryptographic protocols
sections.narration: For real applications, use established protocols and maintained libraries, with proper identity checks and randomness. A neat lock animation can't prove a system is secure. The code, keys, and protocol rules all have to work together too.
bullets: A visual analogy is not a security proof
sections.takeaway: A sound implementation must preserve the whole protocol’s security assumptions.

sections.title: Solve the secrecy puzzle
sections.narration: Here's our final picture: symmetric protection handles the data, public-key tools help establish keys, and authentication checks the right identities and protected message. Secure communication is a team effort. One impressive-looking lock doesn't do every job by itself.
bullets: Combine key setup and data protection
sections.takeaway: Secure communication combines confidentiality, integrity, and sound key handling.
